tur70-1: This is not a diagnosis. The study shows that the death rate in the following years was higher among those who could not do the test; but this is an association, and the test itself does not indicate any disease. The researchers note that they could not account for factors such as recent falls and physical activity. You can treat the test as a warning light, start working on your balance and, if you are concerned, talk to your doctor. The UK’s 2025 falls guideline (NICE) also advises against using falls risk prediction tools to predict the risk of falling; according to the guideline, balance and gait tests help to spot problems with balance but do not predict a person’s risk of falling.

tur70-4: In a meta-analysis combining 47 randomised controlled trials, structured exercise programmes lasting at least 12 weeks (23 trials) lowered HbA1c by an average of 0.67 points: aerobic exercise by 0.73, resistance exercise by 0.57 and programmes combining the two by 0.51 points. Programmes with more than 150 minutes of exercise a week were associated with a fall of 0.89 points, and those with 150 minutes or less with a fall of 0.36 points (a comparison between trials). Advice to “be more active” on its own did not lower HbA1c unless it was given together with dietary advice. The researchers judged the overall quality of the trials to be low.
